en.title: Hope: Is Na Hong-jin's Latest a Glorious Mess or a Masterpiece?
en.summary: Na Hong-jin's new sci-fi action thriller, **Hope**, has arrived, leaving audiences and critics grappling with its polarizing nature. Is it a triumph of visceral filmmaking, or a narrative misfire?
en.body:
South Korean auteur **Na Hong-jin**, known for his intense thrillers like **The Chaser** and **The Wailing**, returns with **Hope**, an ambitious sci-fi action spectacle that has ignited a fervent debate. Premiering at Cannes and now making its way to wider audiences, the film centers on a remote village police chief and his deputy battling a mysterious creature amidst severed communications and a hunting party gone awry. Early reactions reveal a stark division: **Hope** is undeniably a technical marvel in its action sequences, yet frustratingly hollow in its storytelling.

The film's core conflict arises from its narrative structure, which, according to some critics, feels more like two extended chase scenes punctuated by a thematic declaration. The central idea, that "man is the real monster," is reportedly laid bare, undermining the suspense and emotional investment in the characters' survival. Compounding this, certain protagonists exhibit an almost supernatural invulnerability, robbing audiences of the catharsis of seeing them face genuine peril. If you’re seeking a tightly woven plot, **Hope** might leave you wanting.

## A Spectacle of Contrasts

Despite its narrative shortcomings, **Hope** is being lauded for its sheer filmmaking prowess. The cinematography, set design, and editing are frequently praised as exceptional, creating a visually arresting experience. However, this aesthetic brilliance is often juxtaposed with special effects that are widely described as subpar, leading to a jarring disconnect. This duality has left many viewers, including critics like Reuben Baron of Reactor Mag, in a state of bewilderment. Is the film's power derived from its exhilarating, albeit flawed, execution, or is it a case of a poorly constructed film that happens to be incredibly fun to watch?

## The Fan Divide

For fans of **Na Hong-jin**'s previous work and genre filmmaking enthusiasts, **Hope** presents a compelling, if confusing, proposition. The sheer audacity of its action set pieces and the undeniable visual flair have captivated many, even as they acknowledge the film's narrative weaknesses. The consensus seems to be that **Hope** is a film that demands to be experienced, preferably with an engaged audience ready to embrace its chaotic energy. The debate rages on whether its strengths in action and atmosphere outweigh its narrative flaws, making it a truly unique cinematic event that will likely be discussed for years to come.

## What's Next

While **Hope** is currently rolling out to theaters globally, details regarding its streaming release and further distribution plans are still emerging. Audiences are encouraged to seek out the film in cinemas to fully appreciate its ambitious scale and kinetic energy, and to form their own opinions on its polarizing blend of spectacle and story.

Six decades of Doctor Who can attest to that. So let’s start off this review by acknowledging that Na Hong-jin’s alien invasion film Hope barely has a story. It’s two long-ass chase scenes with a sequel tease on top. The characters are ciphers. The film’s single thematic idea (“man is the real monster”) gets spelled out between the two chases, which kills our rooting interest in whether the human protagonists make it to the end, and some of those humans are so stupidly invulnerable we don’t even get the satisfaction of seeing the aliens kill them. If you’re watching Hope for a plot, it’s easy to dismiss. Here’s where I’m conflicted: accepting that Hope is a stupid and shallow movie, is it also an awesome one? On a visceral level, this is an amazing accomplishment in action movie directing. It’s exciting and often beautiful… when it’s not hilariously ugly. The cinematography, set design, and editing kick ass—while the special effects just look like ass. I enjoyed Hope up until its non-ending completely jumped the shark, but before then, I’m conflicted whether this enjoyment was the result of a bad movie that was awesome or a good movie that sucked. The half-hour or so before we see the aliens is unambiguously good. It’s got a great set-up of mystery and suspense—something is causing death and destruction in the town of Hope, and police chief Ko Bum-seok (Hwang Jun-min) has to find what’s causing it while outrunning the damage. Reminiscent of Spielberg having to hide the shark in Jaws , keeping the aliens off-screen for the opening act of Hope only makes the action scarier, and the sheer scale of damage the aliens cause from out of frame raises the stakes even further.
